 A ‘unique 20th Century Israelite’ who always made sure we got it right
 Remembering Capers Funnye who mainstreamed the fact that Blackness and Judaism are not mutually exclusive.

 Rabbi Capers Funnye recites the wedding vows to Gene Pelikhov and Erin Washington in Lynn, Massachusetts on May 22, 2011. Erin is the daughter of the Forward’s Robin Washington. Courtesy of Erin Pelikhov 
 Editor-at-Large 
 Robin Washington 
 November 3, 2026 
 It’s fitting that I first met Rabbi Capers Funnye in a television studio. And it should surprise no one that the topic that brought us together — by no means accidentally — was a discussion about Black Jews.
 We never stopped talking about it. And making sure others got it right.
 The spiritual leader for decades of Chicago’s Beth Shalom B’nai Zaken Ethiopian Hebrew Congregation and since 2016 the Chief Rabbi of the International Israelite Board of Rabbis , Funnye died Nov. 2 at 74.
 Our friendship spanned decades, beginning before we co-founded the Alliance of Black Jews with Michelle Stein-Evers Frankl in 1995. With Stein-Evers, then in Los Angeles, and me in Boston, the organization brought together Jews of African descent from around the country to celebrate our dual affiliations as normative.
 Although the organization did not last beyond its early years, it spawned numerous other groups that exist today. Most significantly, it mainstreamed the fact that Blackness and Judaism are not mutually exclusive.
 -->
 That’s the message we had been imparting five years earlier, on the Black Entertainment Television show Our Voice s in 1990. Having filed a story mentioning Black Jews while a reporter for BET’s news division, I was asked by the network to co-produce a special on the subject. In addition to me, they asked who else should appear.
 “There’s a rabbi in Chicago,” I said unhesitatingly, though I had yet to meet him, “and the police chief in Charleston, South Carolina” — Reuben Greenberg , who passed away in 2014.
 Participants at the 1995 founding meeting of the Alliance of Black Jews in Los Angeles, California (clockwise from top left: Courtenay Edelhart, Robin Washington, Laurence Thomas, Rabbi Capers Funnye, Jr., and Michelle Stein-Evers Frankl. Courtesy of Robin Washington 
 Each of us came to Judaism differently: me, the child of a non-Jewish African-American father and non-Black Jewish mother; Greenberg, via conversion first through Reform, then Conservative Judaism (and also “reversion” in that he was reaching back to the religion of his grandfather), and Funnye, who had been Methodist before joining the Ethiopian Hebrew denomination (of African Americans, not Ethiopians) and later underwent a Conservative conversion.
 Although his smicha was granted by the Ethiopian Hebrew group (now more broadly termed Israelite) and not by the Conservative body, he was invited to join the Chicago Board of Rabbis as its first African American member in 1997.
 His dual affiliations as both Conservative and Israelite — and indeed, that of his largely Black and increasingly Hispanic Chicago shul, which also had merged with an aging Ashkenazi congregation — allowed him to serve as a bridge between many strains of Judaic practices.
 -->
 “He accomplished what he wanted,” said Rabbi Baruch A. Yehudah of Congregation B’nai Adath Kol Beth Yisrael in New York. “He wanted to be a bridge builder and he built many — into the Ethiopian community, the Nigerian community, South Africa, Ghana, Uganda. He was the first one of us to be on a mainstream board of rabbis.”
 “I loved him,” Yehudah added. “He wasn’t just my boss.”
 Bruce Haynes, author of The Soul of Judaism , called Funnye “the most unique 21st Century Israelite” because of his role as chief rabbi. “To my knowledge, that (position) was the first of its kind. It elevated him institutionally as the premiere figure among modern-day Hebrew Israelites.”
 Yet that outreach went beyond the bima. “Having chosen to move his whole family toward Conservative Judaism was an important step in cementing a personal relationship between Israelite congregations and rabbinic Judaism,” Haynes said.
 Rabbi Tamar Manasseh , a protégé of Funnye who in 2021 became the first woman ordained by the Israelite body , said Funnye was “doing the whole bridge thing before anybody knew that they wanted a bridge.
 “There were Black Jews who didn’t like that. There were white Jews who didn’t like that, either. It was uncomfortable for everybody until it wasn’t uncomfortable for anybody.”
 She praised him for enduring “all of the stuff he had to go through to get us to a point where I can complain about things now, which is remarkable.”
 I too find it difficult to separate the personal from the bridge-building. In addition to our numerous Black Jewish campaigns and initiatives — we literally traveled the world together, from Chicago to Boston to San Francisco to Uganda — he served as the rabbi for my mother’s funeral and my daughter’s wedding.
 In my ever-diverse family, both were examples of bridge-building in their own right. During the wedding, my now son-in-law, whose native language is Russian, recited the line “I concentrate you to me as my wife,” prompting Funnye to break from the prepared liturgy to correct him.
 “No, no. Consecrate . We gotta get this right.”
 “I consecrate you to me as my wife,” the groom said, appreciative of the gentle but authoritative guidance.
 Because Capers made sure to get it right.
